title: Two Axes of LLM Abstention: Correctness and Answerability
hook: An LLM should refuse two different things — wrong answers, and questions it shouldn't answer at all. A single confidence score can't tell these apart, but a hidden-state probe can.
key_points: A model should refuse for two distinct reasons: it would get the answer wrong, or the question itself is unanswerable or rests on a false premise.

Across 5 instruction-tuned models (2B-14B, 3 families), ordinary answer-confidence tracks correctness but is nearly blind to whether a question is answerable — and this blind spot doesn't shrink with scale.
It's worst on naturally occurring false-premise questions: confidence, P(IK), P(True), and even asking the model outright all stay near chance, while a hidden-state probe reaches 0.69-0.77 AUROC.
Instructing a model to check premises backfires — it disputes true and false premises alike (57% false challenges); routing that instruction through the probe roughly triples challenge precision.

Combining an answerability probe with a correctness score into a calibrated policy certifies both budgets at once — reaching 0.75 coverage of correct answers vs. 0.31 for a single threshold, and is the only policy that certifies at all at 14B.
content_html: Ask an LLM a question it can't or shouldn't answer, and you'd hope it says so. This paper argues that "hope it says so" is really two separate problems being treated as one.
extra_html: The usual approach thresholds a single confidence score to decide when to refuse — but that conflates two different judgments: would I get this wrong? and should this even be answered? (because it's unanswerable, or rests on a false premise). Testing five instruction-tuned models from three families, spanning 2B to 14B parameters, the author finds these really are separate axes: ordinary answer-confidence tracks correctness well but is nearly blind to answerability, and this gap doesn't close with scale. It's worst on naturally occurring false-premise questions (the CREPE dataset), where confidence, P(IK), P(True), and even directly asking the model whether a premise is false all hover near chance — while a linear probe on hidden states reaches 0.69 to 0.77 AUROC, meaning the model represents a problem internally that it won't report out loud. Instructing the model to check premises doesn't fix this either: it then challenges true and false premises indiscriminately (57% false challenges on sound questions), though routing that instruction through the probe's signal roughly triples challenge precision. Turning both signals into a calibrated policy — requiring an answerability score and a correctness score to each clear their own bar — certifies reliability budgets on both fronts at once, reaching 0.75 coverage of correct answers versus 0.31 for a single threshold, and at 14B it's the only policy tested that certifies at all. Benedikt J. Wagner, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop?
related.hook: Across 28,000+ tasks, agents often can't tell when to quit — some never give up when they should, others bail out only after dozens of wasted tool calls.

related.title: Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action
related.hook: Probes that seem to detect an LLM's harmful intent before it acts mostly just detect the prompt's topic — three careful tests find they don't predict future misbehavior.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two distinct reasons an LLM should refuse to answer, per this paper?
flashcards.back_html: Because it would get the answer wrong (a correctness problem), or because the question itself shouldn't be answered at all — it's unanswerable or rests on a false premise (an answerability problem).

flashcards.prompt: How does ordinary answer-confidence perform on detecting unanswerable or false-premise questions?

choices.text: It's nearly blind to answerability, and this blind spot persists even at larger scale
It detects unanswerable questions perfectly, better than correctness
It improves steadily and closes the gap by 14B parameters

flashcards.explanation_html: Confidence tracks whether an answer is right, but barely tracks whether the question should be answered at all — and scaling the model up doesn't fix this.

flashcards.prompt: Why does instructing a model to 'check premises before answering' backfire?
flashcards.back_html: The model can't reliably tell true premises from false ones once told to look, so it disputes both — 57% of its premise challenges are false alarms on sound questions.

flashcards.prompt: How much does combining a hidden-state answerability probe with a correctness score improve reliable coverage, vs. a single confidence threshold?

choices.text: 0.75 coverage of correct answers vs. 0.31 for a single threshold
No improvement — both reach the same coverage
It only helps at the smallest model size

flashcards.explanation_html: The combined policy — an answerability probe plus a correctness score, each required to clear its own bar — reaches far higher coverage while still certifying both the wrong-answer and unanswerable-answer rates; at 14B it's the only policy that certifies at all.
